Hebrew: וַיִּ֩צֶר֩ יְהֹוָ֨ה אֱלֹהִ֜ים מִן־הָֽאֲדָמָ֗ה כָּל־חַיַּ֤ת הַשָּׂדֶה֙ וְאֵת֙ כָּל־ע֣וֹף הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וַיָּבֵא֙ אֶל־הָ֣אָדָ֔ם לִרְא֖וֹת מַה־יִּקְרָא־ל֑וֹ וְכֹל֩ אֲשֶׁ֨ר יִקְרָא־ל֧וֹ הָֽאָדָ֛ם נֶ֥פֶשׁ חַיָּ֖ה ה֥וּא שְׁמֽוֹ:

- יְהֹוָה = Awtsmoos
- אֱלֹהִים = Elokim
- "formed" - יִּצֶר - this is correct
- "from the earth" - מִן־הָֽאֲדָמָ֗ה - correct


- "every beast of the field" - כָּל־חַיַּ֤ת הַשָּׂדֶה֙ - correct
- "and every fowl of the heavens" - וְאֵת֙ כָּל־ע֣וֹף הַשָּׁמַ֔יִם - correct
- "and He brought [it] to man" - וַיָּבֵא֙ אֶל־הָ֣אָדָ֔ם - correct
- "to see what he would call it" - לִרְא֖וֹת מַה־יִּקְרָא־ל֑וֹ - correct
- "and whatever the man called each living thing" - וְכֹל֩ אֲשֶׁ֨ר יִקְרָא־ל֧וֹ הָֽאָדָ֛ם - correct
- "that was its name" - נֶ֥פֶשׁ חַיָּ֖ה ה֥וּא שְׁמֽוֹ - "that is its name" - the Hebrew uses "that" as a demonstrative referring to the living thing itself, not "its"

The key distinction is that the Hebrew phrase נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה הוּא שְמוֹ literally means "a living creature, that is its name" - the demonstrative "that" points back to the creature being named, not forward to the name itself. The translation should preserve this structure: "and whatever the man called a living creature, that was its name." יקרא is in the singular form, so man naming them is correct. Let me verify the verb form: יִקְרָא can mean "he will call" or "he calls," and since Adam is singular, this aligns. The existing translation "he would call" works fine, capturing the sense of each creature being named as it was brought before him. Let me refine this slightly for clarity while keeping the meaning intact. The Hebrew uses בשר in a way that emphasizes flesh as a substance rather than the specific body part, so "flesh" captures it. For the closing phrase, "in its place" is more precise than "under it" since תחתנה literally means "in her place" or "underneath her." The corrected verse reads: "And Awtsmoos Elokim cast a deep sleep upon man, and he slept, and He took one of his ribs, and He closed up flesh in its place."

For verse 22, the Hebrew verb בנה means "built," but in context with creating woman from the rib, "fashioned" or "formed" conveys the action more naturally in English. The phrase "that He had taken from man" clearly expresses possession, and "into a woman" is the correct target. The bringing action uses the feminine form ויבאה, indicating the rib was brought to Adam as the completed woman.

The revised translation: "And Awtsmoos Elokim fashioned the rib that He had taken from man into a woman, and He brought her to man."

For verse 23, זאת means "this" or "this one," not "it." The phrase עצם מעצמי ובשר מבשרי describes bone and flesh as essential substances. The next section continues with the naming convention where the woman is called ishah because she was taken from ish. The verb יקרא uses a feminine form, confirming that man named the woman this way. The clause structure requires completing the thought: "that was its name." This is the standard phrase for naming throughout creation narratives. The phrase "bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh" captures the intimacy Adam feels—these aren't just any bones or flesh, but specifically his own. The demonstrative "this one" points to the woman herself, emphasizing her as the immediate result of his own substance. The Hebrew construction ties everything together: whatever Adam called this living being would become its true name, and in this case, he called her ishah (woman) because she was taken from ish (man). The repetition of "this one" emphasizes the specific nature of what was created from his own body. man was alone in his need for companionship. The divine solution was to create a suitable partner from his own body.

**Refined verse-20:** "And man gave names to all the cattle and to the fowl of the heavens and to all the beasts of the field, but for man, no suitable helper was found opposite him."

The emphasis shifts slightly—"suitable helper" better captures the Hebrew's focus on finding someone who truly met his need, rather than just any companion. The verb יקרא uses the imperfect form, which in Hebrew can express habitual or gnomic action—meaning whenever man encountered a living creature, he named it. The present tense "calls" better captures this sense of general behavior rather than a one-time event. Though "would call" also works, "calls" more directly reflects the Hebrew grammar's aspect. The rest of the verse flows naturally: "and whatever the man called a living creature, that was its name." The overall flow seems more natural with "called" as the present tense form, even though "would call" is technically more precise for the Hebrew aspect. The meaning remains clear either way.

For verse 20, the Hebrew uses בהמה to refer to livestock rather than just cattle, and שדה distinguishes field animals from those in cities or homes. A more accurate translation would be "domestic beasts" or "livestock" to capture this distinction better than the existing "cattle."

Verse 21 has an issue with "under it" — the Hebrew תַּחְתֶּנָה literally means "in her place" or "underneath her," referring to where the flesh was positioned around the rib opening, not beneath the rib itself. "In its place" is the correct rendering.

For verse 22, I need to verify the verb בנה (built/fashioned) and ensure the feminine pronoun אותה refers back to the rib properly.

Looking at the next section, the Hebrew construction אֶת־הַצֵּלָע אֲשֶׁר־לָקַח מִן־הָֽאָדָם uses a relative clause with אֲשֶׁר that requires adjustment—the direct translation is "the rib that He had taken from man," which is awkward in English. Rearranging to "the rib He had taken from man" eliminates the unnecessary "that" and flows more naturally while preserving the meaning.

For the following verse, the structure אִשָּׁה כִּי מֵאִישׁ לֻקֳחָה־זֹּֽאת uses כִּי in a causal sense ("because") rather than emphatic, so the clause should read "she shall be called woman, because she was taken from man." The existing translation's phrasing is less direct and loses this causal relationship.

In verse 24, the Hebrew construction לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד literally means "for one flesh," which in context describes the unity established through marriage rather than a literal physical joining. The phrasing "they shall become one flesh" captures this union more clearly than the existing "become flesh as one," which obscures the intended meaning.

translations.english: And Awtsmoos Elokim formed from the earth every beast of the field and every fowl of the heavens, and He brought each to man to see what he would call it, and whatever the man called a living creature, that was its name.
And man gave names to all the domestic beasts and to the fowl of the heavens and to all the beasts of the field, but for man, no suitable helper was found opposite him.
And Awtsmoos Elokim cast a deep sleep upon man, and he slept, and He took one of his ribs, and He closed up flesh in its place.
And Awtsmoos Elokim fashioned the rib He had taken from man into a woman, and He brought her to man.
And man said, "This time, it is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh. This one shall be called ishah (woman) because this one was taken from ish (man)."
Therefore, a man shall leave his father and his mother, and cleave to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.
